extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, reformers, and social scientists involved in creating or organizing government intelligence/research bureaus
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for creating, staffing, funding, and operating intelligence/research sections in government and large organizations so they can supply usable, independent facts to decision-makers without becoming bureaucratic advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigation and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The only institutional safeguard is to separate as absolutely as it is possible to do so the staff which executes from the staff which investigates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two should be parallel but distinct bodies of men, recruited differently, paid (if possible) from separate funds, responsible to different heads, intrinsically uninterested in each other's personal success. This prevents the investigative staff from becoming a tool of administration and preserves its disinterestedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence based on funds, tenure, access
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence would turn mainly on three points: on funds, tenure, and access to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress or departmental officials can deprive the staff of money, dismiss them, or close the files, the staff becomes its creature. Institutional design must protect these three pillars to ensure genuine independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure funding arrangements (trust fund/sliding scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: No agency of research can be really free if it depends upon annual doles from what may be a jealous or parsimonious Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed devices include a federal charter creating a trust fund and a sliding scale over years based on departmental appropriation; trust fund to cover minimum overhead and capital, sliding scale for growth; funding should be put beyond accidental interference while remaining amendable by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure security (life tenure, liberal pension, dismissal protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure should be for life, with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, sabbatical years for advanced study and training, and dismissal only after a trial by professional colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions similar to those of any non-profit intellectual career should apply so that staff have dignity, security, and freedom of mind needed to do salient work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed access to materials and investigatory powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureau should have the right to examine all papers, and to question any official or any outsider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to materials should be established in the organic act. The bureau should be able to propose accounting methods to the department and, if rejected or violated, to appeal under its charter to Congress. Continuous investigation differs from sensational legislative inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from Congressional committees and departmental heads
rubrics_metrics.description: The intelligence officials should be independent both of the Congressional Committees dealing with that department, and of the Secretary at the head of it; that they should not be entangled either in decision or in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence implies protection from removal, funding manipulation, or file closure by either Congress or department leadership to prevent the staff becoming a creature of political forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative staff must avoid policy advocacy (disinterested expertise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the expert depends upon separating himself from those who make the decisions; the man who takes a line, and meddles with the decision, is soon discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must not care in their expert self what decision is made; if they begin to care too much they see what they wish to see and stop representing the unseen facts faithfully. Their role is to make the invisible visible, not to prescribe policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts should prepare facts for action before ex post facto analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The real sequence should be one where the disinterested expert first finds and formulates the facts for the man of action, and later makes what wisdom he can out of comparison between the decision and the facts organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the academic ex post facto relationship where experts generalize from facts supplied by actors; instead experts should supply properly framed facts to decision-makers and then later analyze outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right form of reporting: translation, simplification, generalization applied to real world
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert must bring the [environmental facts] to the Secretary's desk, with all the elements in such relation that it is as if he were in contact with the [terrain] itself. The expert must translate, simplify, generalize, but the inference from the result must apply in the [field], not merely on the premises of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports must be framed so inferences and recommendations are directly relevant to the real situation under consideration, not only internally coherent within the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional safeguards against becoming a bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts will enjoy power, and their temptation will be to appoint themselves censors, and so absorb the real function of decision. Unless their function is correctly defined they will tend to pass on the facts they think appropriate, and pass down the decisions they approve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural separation of functions, independent funding and tenure, circulation of personnel and data, and transparency reduce risks of ossification, red tape, and bureaucratic self-protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and index numbers for measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly the various staffs would need to adopt, wherever possible, standards of measurement that were comparable. . . . For the value of competition is determined by the value of the standards used to measure it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop index numbers and quantitative devices to compare administration, productivity, efficiency, service, etc., so competition can be directed to ideal ends; better index numbers make comparison between units (shops, factories, schools, departments, states) useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange of records and central clearing house
rubrics_metrics.description: The information [relevant to a problem] is probably scattered through other departments. The Department should be able to call on its own intelligence bureau to assemble the facts in a way suited to the diplomatic problem up for decision. And these facts the diplomatic intelligence bureau would obtain from the central clearing house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a central focal point for assembling and distributing information across departments so duplication is reduced and research is coordinated; this clearing house could become like a national university and be open in many respects to scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use federations and regional coordination where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In its main outlines the principle is equally applicable to state governments, to cities, and to rural counties. The work of comparison and interchange could take place by federations of state and city and county bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate information and research (not necessarily decision) across jurisdictions where regional problems cross legal frontiers; comparable accounting systems enable cooperation while preserving autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin incrementally within existing machinery and educate stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The better way is to introduce into the existing machinery, wherever you can find an opening, agencies that will hold up a mirror week by week, month by month. When the office-holders begin to see themselves — the same facts — the obstruction will diminish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sweeping reorganizations that provoke entrenched resistance. Use visible, regular analysis to educate officials, subordinates, and the public to build goodwill for new practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and training linked to universities and circulation of personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff could be recruited there for the bureaus from among college graduates. . . . a part of the research itself would be done by students, and political science in the universities would be associated with politics in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use university attachments, temporary specialist appointments, student research, and exchange lecturers to train staff, refresh perspectives, and avoid staleness or pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the unseen visible to influence decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: By making the invisible visible, he confronts the people who exercise material force with a new environment, sets ideas and feelings at work in them, throws them out of position, and so, in the profoundest way, affects the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expert's influence comes from reshaping the perceived environment via facts and measurements; this is more effective than direct advocacy and preserves the expert's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect investigative staff from political destruction or sly attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: The financial arrangement should insure the staff against sly destruction, and should at the same time provide for growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate political maneuvers like jokers and riders; design appropriation and charter mechanisms so attacks would have to be made openly, reducing covert sabotage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and accountability mechanisms (right to appeal to Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposal [for accounting methods] is rejected, or violated after it has been accepted, [the bureau should be able] to appeal under its charter to Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an institutional route for the intelligence bureau to contest departmental obstruction or violation of standards, balancing independence with democratic oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance solely on anecdotal, sporadic, or administratively biased data
rubrics_metrics.description: The social scientist assembles his data out of a mass of unrelated material. . . . The student knows this, and as a protection against it, has developed that branch of scholarship which is an elaborated suspicion about where to discount his information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence work should organize and collect comparably recorded, systematic data rather than relying on accident-of-administration records; improved data collection improves the quality and usefulness of expert analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use low-risk, widely distributed experiments to test hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When each school district and budget, and health department, and factory, and tariff is the material of knowledge for every other, the number of comparable experiences begins to approach the dimensions of genuine experiment. . . . there is opportunity for trial and error at such slight risk that any reasonable hypothesis might be given a fair test without shaking the foundations of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the multiplicity of comparable units (states, cities, factories, schools) to run practical tests of policies and administrative techniques with limited risk and high informational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design competition around meaningful standards (select goals and rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is to select the goals of competition and the rules of the game. Almost always the most visible and obvious standard of measurement will determine the rules of the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and provide metrics for the values (efficiency, service, productivity) you want competition to promote; without clear measures competition will target money, power, or popularity rather than social aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain circulation of data and criticism to reduce dry rot
rubrics_metrics.description: But if one could assume that there was circulation through the whole system between government departments, factories, offices, and the universities; a circulation of men, a circulation of data and of criticism, the risks of dry rot would not be so great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote personnel exchanges, shared datasets, and open critique across institutions to prevent pedantry, red tape, and the entrenchment of ineffective practices.
